title: Stracciatella
subtitle: Roman egg-drop soup with Parmesan and nutmeg
excerpt: A Roman classic: beaten eggs, Parmesan, and a little semolina poured in a thin stream into simmering capon or chicken broth and stirred gently until the egg forms soft, irregular strands. Ready in 5 minutes.
sourceNotes: Stracciatella alla Romana is documented in Ada Boni's Il Talismano della Felicità (1929) and appears in multiple Roman cooking references. The dish appears in Pellegrino Artusi's La Scienza in Cucina e l'Arte di Mangiar Bene (1891, public domain) under the name 'minestra di uova' (egg soup). It is one of the oldest and simplest recipes in the Roman culinary canon.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cannot be made ahead: the egg strands become rubbery if the soup sits. Make and serve immediately.

content.text: Stracciatella is one of the quickest soups in Italian cooking. The name means 'little rags' or 'torn pieces': the egg mixture, poured into the simmering broth in a thin stream and stirred gently, sets into soft, irregular shreds. It takes 5 minutes from cold broth to table. The quality of the broth is everything; this is not a dish to make with a stock cube.

items.prepNote: best-quality, ideally homemade capon or chicken broth
finely grated, plus more to serve
or fine breadcrumbs; helps the egg strands hold their shape

content.text: Bring the stock to a simmer in a large saucepan. Taste and adjust the seasoning: the broth is the base of the soup and must be well-seasoned before the eggs go in.
Beat the eggs in a bowl with the Parmesan, semolina, a grating of nutmeg, and a little salt and pepper until smooth.

With the stock at a gentle, steady simmer, pour the egg mixture in a thin, steady stream into the broth, stirring gently and continuously with a fork or a whisk. The egg will set immediately into soft, irregular strands. Stir gently for 1 to 2 minutes. Do not boil vigorously: the egg strands should be soft, not rubbery.
Ladle into warm bowls immediately. Scatter with chopped parsley and serve with extra Parmesan.

items.symptom: Egg forms a single solid mass rather than strands
items.cause: Egg mixture added too quickly, or stock at a rolling boil
items.fix: Pour the egg in a very thin stream with one hand while stirring with the other. The stock should be at a gentle simmer, not a vigorous boil.

items.symptom: Soup tastes flat despite good broth
items.fix: Season the egg mixture with salt, pepper, and nutmeg before adding it. Parmesan is salty but the egg itself needs seasoning.

content.text: Stracciatella is the soup of Rome and Lazio, eaten at Sunday lunch before the main course. It is a warming, light dish for Roman family tables. It is also a convalescent food, given to sick children and elderly grandparents who cannot manage something heavier. A version appears in Jewish-Roman cooking as well as in the mainstream Roman tradition. It is one of the few Italian soups with almost no regional variation. The same recipe appears across Lazio with only minor changes in the proportion of eggs to broth.
